title: Immunology
tagline: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibodies and T cells, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity and vaccines
summary: The immune system defends the body and, when it errs, causes disease. This course covers innate immunity, antigen recognition, B- and T-cell responses, tolerance and regulation, hypersensitivity, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency, transplantation and tumour immunology, and vaccines and immunotherapy.
overview: Immunology explains two everyday facts: why we are not overwhelmed by the microbes we breathe, eat and touch, and why the body does not normally attack itself. The answer has layers. An innate system, present from birth, recognises broad classes of microbe within minutes. An adaptive system of B and T cells learns to recognise individual molecules, takes a week or more to respond the first time, and remembers. Tolerance mechanisms keep the adaptive system from turning on the body's own tissues.

The course follows that structure. It begins with barriers, phagocytes, pattern recognition, complement and inflammation; then the receptors of B and T cells, MHC molecules and antigen presentation; then T-cell activation, helper subsets, antibody production and memory; then central and peripheral tolerance. The second half applies these mechanisms to disease: the four types of hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis; autoimmune disease and the interpretation of autoantibodies; primary and secondary immunodeficiency, including HIV and asplenia; transplant rejection and immunosuppression; tumour immunology and checkpoint, CAR-T and antibody therapies; and vaccines.

Each chapter links mechanism to the clinic: the infection pattern that points to a missing component, the tryptase sample that confirms mast-cell activation, the positive ANA that does not mean lupus, the rising creatinine that may be rejection or BK virus, the herd immunity threshold for measles. Worked clinical cases, quick checks and graded exercises with full solutions run through every chapter. Management is described in principle, with reference to UK guidance where relevant; individual treatment follows current local guidelines.
outcomes: Describe the barriers, cells, pattern-recognition receptors, complement pathways and cytokines of innate immunity, and explain inflammation, fever and the acute-phase response, including the kinetics of CRP.

Explain how antibodies and T-cell receptors recognise antigen, how V(D)J recombination generates receptor diversity, and how MHC class I and class II molecules present peptides to CD8 and CD4 T cells.

Explain T-cell activation by antigen, costimulation and cytokines, the functions of the helper T-cell subsets and cytotoxic T cells, germinal-centre B-cell responses, antibody isotypes and immunological memory, and use them to interpret serology.
Explain central and peripheral tolerance and recognise the monogenic diseases (APS-1, IPEX, ALPS, CTLA-4 haploinsufficiency) that reveal each mechanism.
Classify hypersensitivity reactions into types I to IV by mechanism and timing, outline the recognition and emergency management of anaphylaxis, and interpret tryptase, skin-prick and patch tests.
Explain the multifactorial causes and mechanisms of autoimmune disease, and interpret autoantibody results in the light of pre-test probability.

Recognise the patterns of infection that suggest antibody, T-cell, phagocyte, complement or splenic defects, distinguish primary from secondary immunodeficiency including HIV infection, and outline the first-line investigations.

Explain allorecognition, the types of transplant rejection, the mechanisms and hazards of immunosuppressive drugs, graft-versus-host disease, tumour immune escape, and the principles and toxicities of checkpoint inhibitors and CAR-T cells.

Explain how the main vaccine types and adjuvants generate protection, calculate herd immunity thresholds, evaluate vaccine safety evidence, and describe the mechanisms and risks of therapeutic monoclonal antibodies and other immunotherapies.

history.title: Vaccination
history.detail: Edward Jenner inoculates James Phipps with material from a cowpox lesion and later shows that the boy is protected against smallpox. Vaccination replaces the riskier practice of variolation and, nearly two centuries later, makes the eradication of smallpox possible.

history.title: Phagocytes
history.detail: Élie Metchnikoff sees mobile cells gather around rose thorns pushed into starfish larvae and proposes that phagocytes defend the body. His cellular theory of immunity is opposed for years by supporters of humoral (serum) immunity; both turn out to be right.

history.title: Antitoxin serum therapy
history.detail: Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō show that serum from animals immunised against diphtheria or tetanus toxin protects other animals. Antitoxin is the first antibody to be described and the first serum therapy; Behring receives the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901.

history.title: Anaphylaxis
history.detail: Charles Richet and Paul Portier find that dogs given a second, small dose of a sea-anemone toxin die within minutes. Richet names the phenomenon anaphylaxis, showing that an immune response can harm rather than protect.

history.title: The antiglobulin test
history.detail: Robin Coombs, Arthur Mourant and Rob Race describe the antiglobulin test, which detects antibody coating red cells. It becomes essential for transfusion compatibility testing and for the diagnosis of haemolytic disease of the newborn and autoimmune haemolysis.

history.title: Acquired tolerance
history.detail: Rupert Billingham, Leslie Brent and Peter Medawar show that mice exposed to foreign cells around birth later accept skin grafts from the same donor strain, confirming Burnet and Fenner's prediction that tolerance to self is learned during development.

history.title: Clonal selection
history.detail: Frank Macfarlane Burnet proposes that each lymphocyte carries a single pre-existing receptor and that antigen selects and expands the matching clone. The theory explains specificity, memory and self-tolerance and still frames the subject.

history.title: MHC restriction
history.detail: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty show that cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected cells only when those cells share the animal's own MHC molecules, revealing that T cells recognise antigen together with self MHC.

history.title: Monoclonal antibodies
history.detail: Georges Köhler and César Milstein fuse antibody-producing B cells with myeloma cells to make hybridomas that secrete a single antibody indefinitely. Engineered monoclonal antibodies later become one of the largest classes of medicines.

history.title: The LPS receptor
history.detail: Building on the discovery of Toll's role in fly immunity by Jules Hoffmann's group (1996) and of a human Toll homologue by Ruslan Medzhitov and Charles Janeway (1997), Bruce Beutler's group shows that LPS-resistant mice carry mutations in Tlr4. Pattern recognition, predicted by Janeway, becomes a molecular science.

history.title: Checkpoint inhibition
history.detail: Ipilimumab, an antibody that blocks CTLA-4, is approved for advanced melanoma, followed in 2014 by antibodies against PD-1. James Allison and Tasuku Honjo, whose work identified these inhibitory receptors as targets, share the 2018 Nobel Prize.

references.title: Janeway's Immunobiology
references.authors: Kenneth Murphy, Casey Weaver and Leslie Berg
references.note: Tenth edition. The standard account of the mechanisms of immunity, from innate recognition to memory, clearly illustrated; the reference for the first half of this course.

references.title: Cellular and Molecular Immunology
references.authors: Abul K. Abbas, Andrew H. Lichtman and Shiv Pillai
references.note: Tenth edition. Detailed and precise on lymphocyte development, tolerance and effector mechanisms, with consistent links to disease.

references.title: Roitt's Essential Immunology
references.authors: Peter J. Delves, Seamus J. Martin, Dennis R. Burton and Ivan M. Roitt
references.note: Thirteenth edition. A concise, readable textbook covering basic and clinical immunology, including hypersensitivity, transplantation and vaccines.

references.title: Essentials of Clinical Immunology
references.authors: Helen Chapel, Mansel Haeney, Siraj Misbah and Neil Snowden
references.note: Sixth edition. A UK clinical text organised around patients: immunodeficiency, allergy, autoimmunity and the interpretation of immunological tests.

references.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers
references.note: The UK guideline for recognising and treating anaphylaxis, including intramuscular adrenaline, refractory anaphylaxis and timed tryptase samples.

references.title: Immunisation against infectious disease (the Green Book)
references.note: The UK reference for vaccines, schedules, contraindications and the vaccination of immunosuppressed and asplenic people; chapters are updated individually, so always check the current version online.
